posts.title: Burberry: The Invention of Gabardine & The Trench Coat
posts.excerpt: When protecting yourself against rough weather, your choice of clothing often comes down to a balance between comfort and structural function. posts.content:
Burberry: The Invention of Gabardine & The Trench Coat

When protecting yourself against rough weather, your choice of clothing often comes down to a balance between comfort and structural function. In the modern fashion world, few garments manage to blend industrial utility with high-fashion prestige quite like the Burberry Heritage Trench Coat. Worn by cinematic icons, global royalty, and modern style trailblazers, this single article of clothing has spent over a century as a timeless symbol of sophisticated style.

However, the coat's signature look was not created to capture attention on a fashion runway. Instead, it was engineered as a high-performance piece of military hardware designed to help soldiers survive some of the harshest, most unforgiving environments on Earth. At the center of this fashion revolution was a massive textile breakthrough that altered the outerwear industry forever.

This detailed historical guide explores how founder Thomas Burberry reshaped the garment industry. We will look at the material science behind his proprietary fabric invention, trace the military history that gave the trench coat its name, examine the practical function of its classic design details, and look at how this historic piece evolved into a cornerstone of modern luxury.

The Master Weatherproofer: Thomas Burberry’s Vision

The foundation of the historic brand was built far from the high-end fashion avenues of London. In 1856, a 21-year-old former draper's apprentice named Thomas Burberry opened a modest outdoor apparel shop in Basingstoke, Hampshire. He established his business with a clear, practical focus: clothing should protect people from the famously damp, unpredictable British weather.

During the 19th century, keeping dry in a heavy downpour was an uncomfortable experience. The primary waterproof garments available were made of rubberized oilskins or heavy macintosh fabrics. While these materials were highly effective at blocking rain, they were heavy, stiff, and completely lacked breathability. Anyone wearing them during physical activity quickly found themselves uncomfortably warm and damp from the inside out. Thomas Burberry recognized this massive flaw and spent years experimenting with textile weaving techniques to develop a lightweight material that could repel water while allowing air to circulate freely.

The Evolution of Outerwear Materials

To understand how revolutionary this change was, it helps to look at the transition of fabrics over time. The table below outlines how the invention of gabardine fundamentally solved the limitations of traditional outdoor clothing.

 

 

Era & Fabric Type

 

Core Materials Used

Performance Advantages

Major Design Limitations

Pre-1870s Oilskins

Heavy canvas coated in boiled oil or wax

High water resistance in heavy downpours

Stiff, exceptionally heavy, and prone to cracking over time

Macintosh Fabrics

Layers of cloth bonded with vulcanized rubber

Completely impervious to external rain

Lacked any air circulation, causing extreme internal condensation

1879 Gabardine

Long-staple Egyptian cotton yarn treated before weaving

Lightweight, completely weatherproof, and highly breathable

Required specialized, high-density weaving looms to manufacture

 

 

 

The Invention of Gabardine: A Textile Breakthrough

In 1879, Thomas Burberry perfected his signature invention: gabardine. This revolutionary fabric altered the outerwear market by taking a completely new approach to weatherproofing. Instead of coating a finished piece of cloth in a thick layer of heavy rubber or wax, Burberry chose to weatherproof the material at the individual yarn level.

He took high-quality Egyptian cotton threads and treated them with a specialized, secret waterproofing agent before running them through the loom. He then utilized a tight, diagonal twill weave pattern, packing over 100 interlocking threads per centimeter. This dense weaving structure created a surface where rain and wind could not easily penetrate the tiny spaces between the fibers. Instead, water droplets simply beaded up and rolled off the surface, while the unsealed weave allowed internal body heat and moisture to escape effortlessly.

The innovation was an instant success. Patented in 1888, gabardine quickly became the top choice for polar explorers, aviation pioneers, and military outdoor officers who needed reliable, lightweight protection against extreme environmental conditions.

From Battlefield to Runway: The Trench Coat Timeline

While gabardine provided the ideal raw material, the iconic shape of the coat itself was forged by the grim realities of the First World War. The evolution from functional field gear to a global fashion staple followed a precise chronological path.

The Historic Milestone Sequence

1.The Tielocken Coat Design:1901 — Pre-War Innovation.

Thomas Burberry creates the Tielocken coat, a precursor to the trench coat that featured a streamlined silhouette secured with a single strap and buckle closure rather than buttons.

2.Adapting for Trench Warfare:1914 — Frontline Military Engineering.

The British War Office officially commissions Burberry to adapt the design for officers on the front lines, adding strategic features to meet the intense demands of battlefield conditions.

3.The Silver Screen Icon Era:1940s-1950s — Hollywood Transformation.

Returning soldiers bring their functional coats into civilian life, where Hollywood directors adopt the style, wrapping it around legendary film stars to cement its place in pop culture.

4.The High-Fashion Staple:2026 & Beyond — Modern Luxury Dominance.

The garment cements its status as an immutable luxury icon, meticulously manufactured in British mills while constantly reinterpreted by visionary creative directors on global runways.

 

Anatomy of an Icon: The Function Behind Every Detail

Every stitch and buckle on a classic Burberry trench coat has a historical purpose. Features that modern consumers often view as simple fashion details were originally engineered to serve as vital tools for soldiers on the battlefield.

Understanding the function behind these classic components reveals the deep utility of the design:

·         The Double-Breasted Silhouette: Designed with a generous overlap of fabric across the chest to provide an extra layer of windproofing and protection against cold wind.

·         The Gun Flap (Storm Patch): This extra panel of fabric on the right shoulder was designed to keep rainwater from seeping into the jacket when an officer held their rifle across their chest. It also helped cushion the recoil of the firearm.

·         The D-Ring Belt: The sturdy metal "D"-shaped rings stitched into the waist belt were designed to securely hold military equipment, including maps, water canteens, and necessary tools.

·         Epaulettes on the Shoulders: The buttoned shoulder straps were added to cleanly display an officer's rank insignias without damaging the main body of the coat. They also worked well to secure the straps of binoculars or gas masks.

·         The Back Storm Shield: This unique cape-like flap across the upper back allows rainwater to run cleanly off the coat and hit the ground, keeping the lower back dry during long hours standing in the rain.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Thomas Burberry invent the trench coat alone?

While Thomas Burberry invented gabardine and finalized the iconic trench design used by British officers, the development of the style was a collaborative era effort. The historic British brand Aquascutum also developed high-quality waterproof coats for the military during the same period. However, Burberry’s proprietary fabric tech and signature design elements secured its spot as the ultimate definition of the classic style.

Why is the traditional lining a check pattern?

The famous camel, red, black, and white check pattern—known worldwide as the Burberry Check—was first introduced in the 1920s. Originally, it was used strictly as a humble, utilitarian lining for the interior of their raincoats. It wasn't until the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, when the British team traveled with the coats over their arms, that the public caught a glimpse of the lining, launching it into a global symbol of luxury.

Where are the Heritage Trench Coats manufactured today?

To preserve the absolute authenticity and premium quality of the brand, every single Heritage Trench Coat is manufactured at the company's dedicated manufacturing mill in Castleford, Yorkshire, England. The specialized gabardine fabric itself continues to be woven nearby at the company's historic mill in Keighley.

A Century of Architectural Tailoring

Thomas Burberry’s legacy is a masterclass in combining brilliant material science with functional design. By inventing gabardine and refining the lines of the British military trench coat, he created a design framework that has successfully resisted the fast-moving trends of the fashion industry for generations.

When you invest in a classic trench coat, you are not simply buying a seasonal fashion statement. You are wearing over 140 years of industrial innovation, British military heritage, and meticulous artisan tailoring that remains just as protective and stylish today as it was on the historic fields of the past.

posts.content:
Alexander McQueen (Under Sarah Burton): Technical Mastery & Royal Romance


When Lee Alexander McQueen passed away in 2010, the fashion world held its breath. The brand had always been defined by its founder’s raw, rebellious, and often dark theatricality. Sarah Burton, who had worked closely alongside McQueen for over 14 years, stepped into the role of Creative Director with a monumental task: to honor the house's avant-garde heritage while establishing her own signature. Over her 13-year tenure, Burton did more than just preserve the brand—she evolved it into a powerhouse of technical mastery, refined romanticism, and timeless British elegance.


The Transition: Honoring Heritage While Finding a New Voice


Sarah Burton’s arrival at the helm was a period of delicate transition. The fashion industry watched to see if the brand would lose its "edge" without its founder’s provocative spirit. Instead, Burton leaned into the house's core strength: extraordinary craftsmanship.


While McQueen was known for shock value, Burton shifted the focus toward the sheer beauty of the garment. She proved that the brand did not need to be controversial to be compelling. Her approach was rooted in deep respect for the tailoring techniques that McQueen himself had mastered during his early days on Savile Row. Under her guidance, the brand became a celebration of the artisan, emphasizing the hidden handwork that elevates high fashion into fine art.


The Royal Romance: A Global Cultural Milestone


If there is one moment that solidified Sarah Burton’s place in fashion history, it was the 2011 Royal Wedding. When Catherine, Princess of Wales, chose a Burton-designed gown for her wedding to Prince William, the global perspective on Alexander McQueen changed forever.

Burton’s design for the royal gown was a masterclass in subtlety and historical reverence. It featured intricate lace work created by the Royal School of Needlework, blending traditional Victorian corsetry with a modern, clean silhouette. This moment was crucial for the brand; it showed the world that Alexander McQueen could represent the highest level of formality and grace. Burton’s ability to move from avant-garde runway concepts to royal-grade couture showcased the incredible versatility of the brand's technical team.

 

 

Technical Mastery: The Anatomy of a McQueen Creation


Burton’s work was defined by a devotion to the "how" of fashion. She did not just design a dress; she engineered it. Her collections frequently highlighted the structural integrity of garments, ensuring that every seam, pleat, and embroidery placement served a specific purpose.


To understand what defines a Burton-era McQueen creation, consider these core design pillars:

  • Architectural Tailoring: Burton maintained the house's signature sharp shoulders and cinched waists, creating a silhouette that is instantly recognizable as powerful, structured, and distinctively "McQueen."
  • Hand-Applied Embellishment: A hallmark of her collections was the intense labor of love—often involving thousands of hours of hand-beading, embroidery, and petal-layering—designed to mimic organic forms like flowers, insects, or skeletal structures.
  • Fabric Innovation: She often used heavy, dense fabrics (like structured wools and rigid silks) and manipulated them into surprisingly soft, fluid shapes, demonstrating a level of fabric control that few designers can match.
  • Nature-Inspired Motifs: Moving away from the darker themes of the early 2000s, Burton introduced a softer, nature-focused romanticism, often featuring woodland elements, botanical prints, and earth-toned palettes that celebrated the British landscape.

Legacy and Evolution


Sarah Burton’s contribution to Alexander McQueen is a testament to the idea that a brand can evolve without losing its soul. She took a label known for its explosive, volatile energy and refined it into a house known for its poetic, almost ethereal, technical perfection.

By the time she stepped down in 2023, she had ensured that the house was no longer just defined by the memory of its founder, but by its own continued ability to innovate. She set a standard for technical excellence that will influence the brand’s direction for years to come. Her tenure proved that true creative success is not just about the loud impact of a runway show, but the quiet, rigorous pursuit of the perfect stitch.
